title: Police officer cleared in shooting; Victim continued knife attack after warning issued at gunpoint
article: An Amherstburg police officer has been cleared of any wrongdoing in the shooting death of Robert Scott Carpenter and the early- morning incident will likely be the focus of a coroner's inquest.

"There's a good possibility that there will be an inquest," said Jon Ansell, of the province's special investigations unit, a civilian agency. "It's not certain by any means but it usually happens," he said Thursday.

Eight SIU investigators designated a subject police officer and interviewed four witness police officers and 10 civilians in their three-week investigation of the shooting of Carpenter, a 36-year- old father of two.
Three officers, including a non-uniformed and unarmed officer, were directly involved in the Oct. 30 incident, which began as a domestic dispute between Carpenter and his common-law wife.
Reached by telephone Thursday night, Scott Carpenter, the victim's father, said the family had no comment about the SIU findings and referred questions to Windsor lawyer Pat Ducharme.
Neither Ducharme nor Amherstburg police chief Brian Bird could be reached for comment.
Ansell said the non-uniformed officer was booking off his shift and about to go home when the disrupted 911 call came in about 7 a.m.

Without his gun and without his pepper spray, the officer jumped in a cruiser with a uniformed officer and raced to Carpenter's home at 258 McCurdy Drive to back up an officer who had already arrived to find a highly-charged domestic dispute.
Ansell said police officers are never technically off-duty and that it isn't uncommon for non-uniformed officers to be dispatched to emergency situations.
The call on McCurdy Drive certainly qualified, he said.
"They had no idea what that call was about. It was a 911 call but it was incomplete," said Ansell.
"You send as many men as you can until you know what's going on."
The first uniformed officer arrived within minutes to find Carpenter's common-law-wife Lisa Stewart distraught and requesting assistance.
"Mr. Carpenter met him at the door and wouldn't let him in but he managed to get through and pull the woman outside," said Ansell.
Stewart desperately implored the officer to get her two children - - three-year-old Sarah and two-year-old Noah -- out of the house, said Ansell.
She also told him Carpenter was brandishing a knife.
The officer's pleas for Carpenter to open the locked door fell on deaf ears and a brief standoff ensued.

When the two other officers arrived as backup they assisted their comrade on the porch. When the front door suddenly opened, one of the officers fell onto the foyer floor and was set upon by Carpenter wielding a knife in his right hand, said Ansell.
The officer sustained wounds to his head and chest and a uniformed officer pulled his pistol and ordered Carpenter to drop the knife.
He didn't listen or he didn't hear. He continued to slash at the downed officer.
"Not only does he not drop the knife, he continues the assault," said Ansell.
The officer fired a single shot to protect his fellow officer and it struck Carpenter in the leg. He was rushed to Hotel-Dieu Grace Hospital where he was pronounced dead about three hours later.

Two of the officers were treated and released from Hotel-Dieu Grace Hospital for non-life-threatening injuries but Ansell couldn't say whether Carpenter pounced on the uniformed or non-uniformed officer.
He stressed there were no grounds to believe that Carpenter, confronted on his doorstep in the early morning by a non-uniformed officer, didn't know he was dealing with police officers.

"The first fellow at the door was quite recognizable and identified himself as a police officer," he said. "There shouldn't have been any confusion ... He should have known that police officers were at his door."
